sources.title: Dayananda Saraswati (Q224906), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): English label 'Dayananda Saraswati', description 'Indian social reformer (1824-1883)', instance of human, born 12 February 1824, died 30 October 1883, citizenship British Raj, occupations including philosopher, autobiographer, priest and swami. No Korean label or Korean Wikipedia article exists. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Thomas J. Hopkins, 'Dayananda Sarasvati', Encyclopedia of Religion (1987; reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: scholarly reference entry built on his two autobiographical statements (the longest in The Theosophist, 1879-80) and on Jordens's 1978 biography: childhood probably at Tankara in Kathiawar, loss of faith in image worship at a Shiva temple, flight from an arranged marriage c. 1845, initiation as Dayananda Sarasvati in 1847, 13 years as a wandering yogin, study from 1860 with the Sanskrit grammarian Virajananda (Vrijananda) at Mathura and departure in 1863 committed to the Vedas, 1863-73 debating in small towns along the Ganges in Sanskrit, four months in Calcutta in 1873 where Keshab Chandra Sen advised him to give up the loincloth and Sanskrit, founding of the Arya Samaj in Bombay on 10 April 1875, a breakthrough in the Punjab with a Lahore chapter in 1877, control left to local chapters, and a final revision of the Satyarth Prakash shortly before his death on 30 October 1883. Balanced academic voice.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Dayananda Sarasvati' (read in full). General reference: early revulsion at idol worship, flight from an arranged marriage into the Sarasvati order, discipleship of Virajananda, a public debate with orthodox pandits at Benares before the maharaja, the first Arya Samaj meeting in Bombay on 10 April 1875, social reforms (against child marriage, for widow remarriage, Vedic study open to all castes, educational and charitable institutions), claims about the Vedas that 'seem extravagant' (such as electricity), the reawakening of nationalism, and a death after 'vigorous public criticism of a princely ruler' with a possible poisoning that was never proved in court. Short and celebratory in tone.

J. N. Farquhar, 'Modern Religious Movements in India' (New York: Macmillan, 1915), the section on Dayananda and the Arya Samaj, pp. 104-115 (Internet Archive scan of the University of Michigan copy; read in full for these pages, including plate V). SOURCE FROM A CHRISTIAN MISSIONARY SCHOLAR: his early life from the autobiography and Chhajju Singh's biography; his teacher Virajananda, a blind Panini scholar who made him throw his modern books into the Jumna; his schools financed by well-to-do men that 'came to nothing' because the teaching pandits did not teach his ideas; his change of dress after Calcutta; the 1875 founding on Brahmo and Prarthana models; the Theosophical alliance of 1878-81 that ended in bitterness; the 1882 cow-protection society; his view that the sections on Islam and Christianity in the Satyarth Prakash are among the most unfair in religious controversy; and his doctrine that the Vedas are God's eternal utterance, which Farquhar calls an old dogma. Farquhar rejects the charge that Dayananda was a political schemer. Critical and partisan; used for facts that also appear elsewhere and for the counter-voice.

Lajpat Rai, 'The Arya Samaj: An Account of Its Origin, Doctrines, and Activities, with a Biographical Sketch of the Founder' (London: Longmans, Green, 1915; Internet Archive; read the biography of the founder, the founding and death, and the education chapters, and searched the rest). BY AN ARYA SAMAJ LEADER, so partisan and in places hagiographic, but it reproduces an eyewitness article on the Benares disputation of November 1869 from the Calcutta Christian Intelligencer of March 1870 (by a European Christian missionary who met Dayananda before and after the disputation and signed with initials): he found him 'a good reasoner and pretty fair in controversy', 'extremely authoritative in all his positions', 'an independent student of the Vedas, and free from the trammels of traditional interpretation', but judged the reform likely to fail and his Benares appearance 'a failure' (success only at Farrukhabad). It also quotes Max Mueller on his 'oratorical power' and records the 1885 start of the Dayananda Anglo-Vedic College and the 1891 dispute that led to the Gurukula, both after his death.

Har Bilas Sarda, 'Speeches and Writings' (Ajmer, 1935), the lecture on Dayanand Saraswati (Internet Archive scan; read the lecture and the biographical note on the Paropkarini Sabha). BY A FOLLOWER AND LATER SECRETARY OF THE SABHA, so hagiographic: says that by his will Dayananda created the Paropkarini Sabha, a body of 23 members, to publish and expound the Vedas, to send missionaries to all countries and to give protection and right education to orphans and the poor, that he translated the Vedas' teaching into Hindi so that all could read it, and that he travelled to every important town and pilgrim centre without a headquarters. Used only for the existence and aims of the trust.

'Sarasvati, Dayananda', World Religions Reference Library (Gale; reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). Student-level reference entry: a wandering ascetic who took up public debate with Hindus, Christians and Muslims, the Satyarth Prakash and the Arya Samaj in 1875, the change of dress and language in Calcutta, several attempts on his life, and his advice to the Maharaja of Jodhpur in 1883 followed by a suspected poisoning that was never proved. It also says he called for armed revolution against the British, a claim that conflicts with Hopkins's and Farquhar's accounts and is not used. Derivative and less careful on dates (it has him fleeing home in 1843 and wandering to 1869).

'Dayananda's Arya Samaj', Hinduism Today (March-April 2001; read in full). Magazine piece from a Hindu publication: describes him as a compelling leader who was 'adamant and unyielding', says that no one who knew him 'even his friends' would deny he was antagonistic and confrontational, that he never held the Samaj presidency and was an ordinary member, that he established vegetarianism and prohibited alcohol in the Samaj, and that he faced ridicule and physical abuse. Popular and unsourced; its claim that he partly recanted his rejection of idol worship is not used.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_dayananda_rai, src_dayananda_hopkins, src_dayananda_farquhar, src_dayananda_britannica | 1860-1875 | Arya Samaj leader quoting a 1870 eyewitness, encyclopedia, missionary scholar, general reference] The 1870 eyewitness at Benares calls him 'an independent student of the Vedas, and free from the trammels of traditional interpretation' who held the standard commentary of Sayana of little account; Hopkins says he rejected the Hindu sectarian traditions, not only Vaishnavism but eventually the worship of the formless Shiva, in favour of a united Hinduism based on the Vedas; Farquhar says he gave up the Vedanta doctrine of his early teacher and discarded some Yoga books after testing them against a dissected body (his own account). Against this, the same eyewitness found him 'extremely authoritative in all his positions' and Farquhar calls the Vedas-as-God's-utterance an old dogma he held fast, so the independence is from tradition inside a fixed premise. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK / SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 76 / 0.62 via 74 / 0.58 to 72 / 0.56 because the early-life steps rest on his own autobiographical statements and the counter-reading is documented.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_dayananda_rai, src_dayananda_britannica, src_dayananda_gale, src_dayananda_farquhar, src_dayananda_hinduismtoday | 1869-1883 | Arya Samaj leader, general reference, student reference, missionary scholar, magazine] He faced several hundred pandits in the Benares disputation of November 1869 with few supporters (Rai, and the eyewitness he quotes, who says the pandits jeered when he did not at once answer a question about the word Purana); Rai reports four or five attempts on his life in five years, Gale 'several attempts'; in 1883 he criticised the Maharaja of Jodhpur's conduct, which Britannica, Gale and Rai all tie to his fatal illness, with poisoning alleged but never proved; Farquhar says opponents called him 'violent, loud-tongued and overbearing' and the magazine that even friends found him confrontational. The cost to relationships and to the audience he could reach is real, so impact is dual-edged. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK / SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 80 / 0.64 via 76 / 0.58 to 74 / 0.56 because the Jodhpur episode is one story told three times and the attempts on his life come from Arya Samaj tradition. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 74@0.56 -> 72@0.52. debate episodes are retold by followers and missionary scholars from overlapping accounts; early-life rows rest on his own statements.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_dayananda_farquhar, src_dayananda_hopkins, src_dayananda_rai | 1869-1877 | missionary scholar, encyclopedia, Arya Samaj leader] Farquhar says he drew huge audiences and the ear of the wealthy; Hopkins dates his breakthrough to the Punjab in 1877, among merchants and professionals seeking a defence of Hinduism, after he had started lecturing in Hindi; Rai quotes a report of Max Mueller's on his 'oratorical power of the highest order' and a determined will. Mixed: the 1870 eyewitness judged his Benares appearance 'a failure' with the pandits and found real success only at Farrukhabad, and Farquhar notes that the teaching pandits in his schools did not teach his ideas. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK / SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 70 / 0.56 via 66 / 0.50 to 64 / 0.48 (and to inference) because the audience-size claims come from followers and he failed with his chosen audience in Benares.

persistence.rationale: [src_dayananda_hopkins, src_dayananda_farquhar, src_dayananda_rai | 1845-1883 | encyclopedia, missionary scholar, Arya Samaj leader] He left home in about 1845 and spent some 13 years as a wandering yogin and then three years under Virajananda before taking up public debate, a decade of lecturing in small Ganges towns (1863-73), and, after the first Satyarth Prakash of 1874-75, revised it again shortly before his death in 1883 (Hopkins). Farquhar adds that his early schools failed to spread his ideas and he went on to lectures and books. Early years rest on his own autobiographical statements. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 74 / 0.58 to 70 / 0.54.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_dayananda_hopkins, src_dayananda_farquhar, src_dayananda_rai | 1860-1873 | encyclopedia, missionary scholar, Arya Samaj leader] From 1860 he studied Panini's grammar and Patanjali's commentary for two and a half years with Virajananda at Mathura and, at his teacher's demand, threw his modern books into the river; Hopkins says the guru helped him perfect his Sanskrit; the 1870 eyewitness says he spoke Sanskrit fluently 'though not in very polished style' and had read the Atharva Veda only in fragments. Learning is documented by his own account and one guru's story; the outside observation is mixed. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 72 / 0.56 via 66 / 0.50 to 66 / 0.48 (and to inference) because the study history comes from the autobiographical family.

adaptability.rationale: [src_dayananda_hopkins, src_dayananda_farquhar, src_dayananda_rai, src_dayananda_gale | 1873-1877 | encyclopedia, missionary scholar, Arya Samaj leader, student reference] After four months in Calcutta in 1873 he took Keshab Chandra Sen's advice to give up the loincloth for street clothes and to teach in Hindi rather than Sanskrit (four sources agree on the change of language, three of them also on the dress), and Farquhar and Hopkins describe the Arya Samaj's structure as borrowed from the Brahmo and Prarthana Samajes and Hopkins says it found its audience in the Punjab in 1877. The change concerned style and organisation, not his doctrine on the Vedas, which stayed fixed. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 66 / 0.56 to 64 / 0.52 because one episode (Calcutta 1873) carries most of the row.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_dayananda_britannica, src_dayananda_sarda, src_dayananda_hopkins, src_dayananda_rai | 1869-1883 | general reference, follower's lecture, encyclopedia, Arya Samaj leader] Britannica says he opposed child marriage, advocated widow remarriage, opened Vedic study to all castes and founded educational and charitable institutions; Sarda says that by his will he created the Paropkarini Sabha of 23 trustees to publish the Vedas, send missionaries and educate orphans and the poor, and Hopkins says he left control of the Samaj to local chapters. The aims are documented, but the institutions that grew (the Dayananda Anglo-Vedic College of 1885, the Gurukula) were founded by followers after his death (Rai) and are not credited to him, and the trust is described by a follower. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK / SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 76 / 0.58 via 72 / 0.52 to 70 / 0.50.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_dayananda_farquhar, src_dayananda_hopkins, src_dayananda_sarda | 1868-1883 | missionary scholar, encyclopedia, follower's lecture] He found well-to-do men to pay for Sanskrit schools (which, Farquhar says, came to nothing), went to Calcutta because he was 'anxious to meet Keshab Chandra Sen', founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay on 10 April 1875, published the Satyarth Prakash and his Vedic commentary, and by will set up a trust to continue the publishing and missions (Sarda). The founding is documented by several sources; the schools' failure and the trust's follower-sourced description keep the row moderate. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 74 / 0.56 via 70 / 0.52 (self-calibration: kept at 70 / 0.52).

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_dayananda_hopkins, src_dayananda_britannica, src_dayananda_farquhar, src_dayananda_hinduismtoday | 1845-1883 | encyclopedia, general reference, missionary scholar, magazine] He fled home in about 1845 when his parents arranged a marriage and refused all his life to reveal his family name or place of birth in order to keep his freedom as a renunciant (Hopkins; Farquhar says he told no one his real name until death), he left his guru in 1863 to work on his own, and left the Samaj in the hands of local chapters; the magazine adds he never held its presidency. All of this sits inside the role of a sannyasi, so it is weak evidence for a personal trait. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK / SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 74 / 0.56 via 68 / 0.48 to 66 / 0.46 because the early-life acts come from his own autobiographical statements.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead) / REPLACED after one bounded retry, with a weaker kind: the lead, Commons 'Swami Dayananda Saraswati 1911.jpg' (802 x 1160, Andhra Patrika ugadi issue of 12 April 1911, PD-India), is a halftone of a retouched sannyasi portrait seated before a painted waterfall backdrop with the Devanagari caption 'Shrimat Dayanand Saraswati Swamiji'; the newspaper is the only provenance, no photograph or holder is named and the image is plainly not an unretouched lifetime photograph, so it was not used. Other routes tried: Commons 'Dayananda Saraswati.jpg' (315 x 545, a turbaned photograph credited to 'Srijut Krishnaravji, Jabalpur 1874', PD-old-100, no source cited; unverifiable and too small); Lajpat Rai's 1915 frontispiece (stated to be from an oil painting); Durga Prasad's 1908 Satyarth Prakash translation (no portrait in the front matter); a Telugu 'Mahapurushula Jeevitamulu' halftone (very poor); Sri Aurobindo site and Pritchett pages (no source or date). FINAL: plate V (upper picture, 'After his visit to Calcutta') of Farquhar's 'Modern Religious Movements in India' (New York: Macmillan, 1915), facing p. 109, in the Internet Archive scan (item modernreligious01farqgoog, marked not in copyright). IDENTITY: printed caption 'DAYANANDA SARASVATI / After his visit to Calcutta' under the picture; the text of p. 109 refers to 'a picture which still survives' of his post-Calcutta dress; the preface credits the Arya Samaj, Lahore for permission. HOLDER RECORD: no institutional record exists for the underlying picture (the original is not located); the book is the authoritative record and the only holder named is the Arya Samaj, Lahore, credited for permission in 1915; no restriction or contradiction found (no bot walls). KIND historical_depiction: the book calls it a picture, the medium is unstated and the reproduction appears retouched, so it is not claimed to be an unretouched lifetime photograph; likeness could be argued but is not verified. Dimensions 408 x 548 (embedded plate image 560 x 420, rotated and trimmed, greyscale, not upscaled) are small, an acknowledged limitation; the other image on the plate ('As a sannyasi') is the retouched seated-ascetic type and was not used. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-13, Wikidata API) Q224906 label 'Dayananda Saraswati', description 'Indian social reformer (1824-1883)', human, born 12 February 1824, died 30 October 1883; no Korean label or Korean Wikipedia page; no existing candidate with this slug or QID. REGION south_asia, nationality IN, era 19th_century. KOREAN NAME 다야난다 사라스와티 is a transliteration chosen by the researcher and needs a Korean reviewer check. ZERO POLITICS: scored on religious reform, scholarship and teaching conduct only; the 'nationalism' framing (Britannica, Gale) and the 1882 cow-protection society are not scored, and Gale's claim that he called for armed revolution conflicts with Hopkins and Farquhar and is not used. ATTRIBUTION: attributable for his own acts (debates, books, the founding of the Arya Samaj, the will) but limited for institutions: the Dayananda Anglo-Vedic College (1885), the Gurukula, the Arya Samaj's later growth and school network were built by later leaders (Rai) and are not credited to him; his Vedic schools financed by backers 'came to nothing' (Farquhar); the Paropkarini Sabha is known only from a follower's lecture (Sarda), with no date given, so no founding year is carded. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Hopkins, 'Dayananda Sarasvati', Encyclopedia of Religion (1987) (src_dayananda_hopkins). READ (8 sources besides Wikidata): Hopkins (full), Britannica (full), Farquhar pp. 104-115 and plate V, Rai 1915 (founder's biography, Benares account, founding and death, education chapters; the rest searched), Sarda 1935 lecture (the lecture and the Sabha note), Gale student entry (full), Hinduism Today (full), the Book Review India excerpt of Bhattacharya's review of Jordens (only the free opening paragraph was available; not used for any row). Not opened: Jordens 1978 and Jones's Arya Dharm (known only through the reference entries), Chhajju Singh's life (via Farquhar), the Satyarth Prakash itself (the 1908 Durga Prasad translation was opened only for its front matter), Lekh Ram. A Wikipedia mirror seen in search results was not used. PERSPECTIVES: academic reference (Hopkins), general reference (Britannica, Gale), Christian missionary scholar (Farquhar), Arya Samaj leader and follower (Rai, Sarda), a 1870 missionary eyewitness reproduced by Rai, a Hindu magazine. SOURCE FAMILIES: about four (autobiographical statements with Hopkins and Jordens; the 1870 eyewitness; Farquhar with Chhajju Singh; the Arya tradition of Rai, Sarda and Hinduism Today), with Britannica and Gale derivative; the early-life rows depend on the autobiographical family, so no row exceeds 0.56. CONTRADICTIONS: dates of his flight from home (1843, 1845, 1846), initiation (1847 or 1848) and the Calcutta visit (1873 per Hopkins and Farquhar; 1869 per Rai) differ and are not carded beyond 'in 1873'; first Satyarth Prakash 1874 (Farquhar) or 1875; Rai's heroic account of the Benares debate versus the eyewitness's account of jeering pandits and a failure at Benares; the Jodhpur illness and death at Ajmer with a suspected poisoning that was never proved. NOT SCORED: leadership_drive (he held no office and left control to local chapters, so the evidence is ambiguous), collaboration (the Theosophical alliance ended in bitterness but the evidence is thin), analytical_rigor (the eyewitness calls him pretty fair in controversy while Farquhar finds the Satyarth Prakash's critiques of Islam and Christianity extremely unfair), belief_updating. SELF-CALIBRATION: 9 rows scored; the concentration check lowered all 9; self-calibration lowered 5 further (independent_thinking, conflict_tolerance, persuasiveness, impact_motivation, autonomy_need); proactive_agency was reviewed and kept. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: cards (1) founding of the Arya Samaj (1875), (2) Satyarth Prakash, (3) Vedic commentary and the trust for publishing Vedic works and educating the poor. dayananda-saraswati:conflict_tolerance RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 74@0.56 -> 72@0.52. debate episodes are retold by followers and missionary scholars from overlapping accounts; early-life rows rest on his own statements.

portrait.source: Halftone plate V, captioned 'Dayananda Sarasvati. After his visit to Calcutta', facing page 109 of J. N. Farquhar, 'Modern Religious Movements in India' (New York: Macmillan, 1915); the preface thanks 'The Arya Samaj, Lahore' for permission to publish the portrait, and the text on page 109 says that 'a picture which still survives' shows that after his Calcutta visit (1873) he took to regular clothes in the manner of the Brahmo leaders. The medium and maker of the original picture are not stated, and the reproduction looks retouched. Internet Archive scan of the University of Michigan copy (digitised by Google); the file is the image embedded in the scan (560 x 420 pixels), turned upright and trimmed of its frame to 408 x 548, converted to greyscale, not upscaled.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: published in New York in 1915 (before 1931); the original picture's maker is unknown and the Internet Archive record marks the book not in copyright; the Arya Samaj, Lahore is credited only for permission in 1915
portrait.attribution: Unknown maker, picture of Dayananda Sarasvati (after his 1873 visit to Calcutta), supplied by the Arya Samaj, Lahore; reproduced as plate V in J. N. Farquhar, Modern Religious Movements in India (New York: Macmillan, 1915), Internet Archive scan (cropped).
